232.title: Pirkei Avot
232.hook: a short tractate of sayings, read on summer Shabbat afternoons for centuries
232.howItsDone: Many Jews study one chapter of Pirkei Avot each Shabbat afternoon from Passover through the summer; each chapter is traditionally introduced with the line that all Israel has a share in the world to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday, we closed camp four: fourteen Torah portions, read one at a time, and a line to take with you, the cycle keeps turning. Today, camp five begins. The depths: the wisdom underneath. Day two hundred thirty-two.

Everyone has a few sentences they live by. Something a grandmother said at a kitchen table. A line from a coach. A sticky note on the fridge that's been there so long it's gone yellow. They're short, they're portable, and they show up exactly when you need them. For about eighteen hundred years, Jews have had a whole little book of those sentences. It's not long. You could read it in an afternoon. And that's exactly when many Jews do read it: on Saturday afternoons, in the long, slow light of summer. Today: the book of sayings.
screen: `A SENTENCE YOU LIVE BY.` → `A WHOLE BOOK OF THEM.` → `SUMMER SATURDAY AFTERNOONS.`

segments.voice: It's called Pirkei Avot. Chapters of the fathers, or, as it's often called in English, the Ethics of the Fathers. Avot, fathers, means the founding teachers, the sages who shaped Jewish life. It's part of the Mishnah, the great collection of Jewish oral law, gathered around the year two hundred by Rabbi Judah the Prince. The Mishnah is mostly law: how to keep the Sabbath, how to settle a lawsuit, how to plant a field. Avot is the strange one. Almost no law at all. Just sayings, passed from teacher to student over centuries, each with the teacher's name attached. And here's a curious detail. The rabbis didn't place it in the section about prayer or holidays. They put it in the section on damages and courts. One explanation: the people who judge others most need to hear it. The custom of reading it grew over time. Many communities read one chapter each Shabbat afternoon between Passover and Shavuot, six weeks for six chapters. Many keep going all summer, around and around, until the fall holidays. It's printed in most Jewish prayer books. You may already know a line from it without knowing where it came from. Hillel's three questions, for example: if I'm not for myself, who will be? If I'm only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? That's Avot. Over the next weeks, we'll read it the way it's meant to be read. One saying at a time. Slowly.
screen: `CHAPTERS OF THE FATHERS.` · `A MISHNAH WITH ALMOST NO LAW.` · `PLACED AMONG THE COURTS.` · `ONE CHAPTER, ONE SHABBAT.` · then, large: `WISDOM IN SMALL SAYINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one saying slowly. Take Hillel's three questions. Settle, and breathe. First: if I'm not for myself, who will be? Let it sit. Then: if I'm only for myself, what am I? Let that one sit too. Then: if not now, when? Don't answer them. Just turn them over, one at a time, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. The bell holds the time.
Pirkei Avot. Chapters of the fathers: the Mishnah's small book of sayings, read on summer Sabbath afternoons.
Your line: wisdom in small sayings. Today, pick one short sentence, Hillel's or your grandmother's, and carry it with you until tonight. Day two hundred thirty-two.

233.title: The chain (Avot 1:1)
233.hook: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on: Joshua, elders, prophets, the Great Assembly
233.howItsDone: Jewish learning is traditionally passed from teacher to student, and many Jews cite a teaching in the name of the person they learned it from, a practice Avot itself praises.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pirkei Avot: the Mishnah's little book of sayings, read on summer afternoons. Your line was wisdom in small sayings. Did you carry one sentence all day? Today, we open it to the very first line. Day two hundred thirty-three.

Think about how you learned to make your family's best dish. Probably not from a cookbook. Somebody showed you. And they learned it from somebody who showed them. If you traced it back, you'd find a line of hands, each passing it to the next, adjusting a little, keeping the heart of it. Most books of wisdom open with the wisdom. This one doesn't. Before a single piece of advice, Pirkei Avot stops to answer a question: where did this come from? Who handed it to whom? Today: the chain.
screen: `THE FAMILY RECIPE.` → `A LINE OF HANDS.` → `WHERE DID THIS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Avot, in paraphrase. Moses received Torah from Sinai, and handed it to Joshua. Joshua handed it to the elders. The elders to the prophets. And the prophets handed it to the men of the Great Assembly. That's it. A list of hands. Two Hebrew verbs carry the whole thing. Kibbel: he received. And masar: he handed over. Kibbel is the root of the word kabbalah, which at first simply meant tradition: what's been received. Masar gives us masorah, the passing down. Notice a few things the rabbis noticed. It says Moses received Torah, without the word the. Many commentators say that's on purpose: not just the written scroll, but the teaching, the explanations, the way to live it. The oral part, which you can only get from a person. And every link is a person. Joshua, Moses's student. The elders who led after him. The prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest. And the Great Assembly, which tradition says gathered in Ezra's time, after the exile in Babylon. By the end of this chapter, the chain will run all the way down to named rabbis, teacher after teacher. And there's a reason Avot begins here. Everything that follows, be patient, be kind, find a teacher, isn't one clever person's opinion. It arrived through hands. Which means that the day you teach anyone anything, you're a link too.
screen: `MOSES RECEIVED TORAH FROM SINAI.` · `KIBBEL AND MASAR.` · `JOSHUA, ELDERS, PROPHETS, ASSEMBLY.` · `EVERY LINK IS A PERSON.` · then, large: `HANDED DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank one of your teachers. Settle, and breathe. Think back to someone who handed you something that stuck. Not always a classroom teacher. A boss, an aunt, an older kid on the bus, a coach who told you the truth. Picture them. What did they hand you? Now trace it one link back: who do you think handed it to them? Hold both of them for a moment, gratefully. The bell holds the time.
The chain. Avot's first line: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on, hand to hand, to Joshua, the elders, the prophets and the Great Assembly.
Your line: handed down. Today, send a short thank-you to one person who taught you something, and tell them what it was. Day two hundred thirty-three.

234.title: Be slow to judge (Avot 1:1)
234.hook: the Great Assembly: be deliberate in judgment, raise many students, build a fence round the Torah
234.howItsDone: Jewish law sets out careful procedures for courts, including questioning witnesses closely and, in capital cases, delaying any guilty verdict until the next day, and Avot's call to judge deliberately is often applied to everyday life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chain: Moses received Torah at Sinai and it was handed down, all the way to the Great Assembly. Did you thank a teacher? Today, that last link finally speaks. Day two hundred thirty-four.

It takes about a second. You see a screenshot, a headline, a neighbor's car parked badly, a coworker's short email. And the verdict is in. Guilty. Rude. Lazy. Clueless. We judge faster than we breathe, and the internet has made it a sport. Now picture a council of sages, the Great Assembly, at the end of that long chain from Sinai. They've been handed everything. And when Avot finally gives them a voice, the very first word of advice they pass on is about speed.
screen: `THE ONE-SECOND VERDICT.` → `GUILTY, RUDE, LAZY.` → `THE FIRST ADVICE IN AVOT.`

segments.voice: The men of the Great Assembly, Avot says, said three things. Be deliberate in judgment. Raise up many students. And make a fence around the Torah. Three short lines, and the first one is our word today. In Hebrew, hevu metunim ba-din. Metunim means slow, measured, patient. It's the kind of slowness of someone who takes a second look. They were speaking first to judges, the people who decide real cases. And Jewish law built that slowness into its courts. The Mishnah says that in a capital case, the old high court could acquit a person on the same day, but it could not convict on the same day. A guilty verdict had to wait until tomorrow, so the judges would sleep on it and look for any merit they'd missed. Mercy could be quick. Condemnation had to be slow. The other two sayings fit around this one. Raise up many students: don't hoard what you know. One old story says the school of Shammai wanted to teach only the worthy, and the school of Hillel said teach everyone. And make a fence around the Torah: add a little margin of care, so you don't stumble over the line itself. But the order matters. Before students, before fences: slow down. Most of us aren't judges in a court. But we judge all day long. Our kids, our partners, strangers on a train. The first advice of the sages is simply this: whatever verdict you're about to reach, let it wait a moment longer.
screen: `THREE THINGS FROM THE ASSEMBLY.` · `METUNIM — SLOW AND MEASURED.` · `ACQUIT TODAY, CONVICT TOMORROW.` · `STUDENTS AND A FENCE.` · then, large: `JUDGE SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: slow down one judgment. Settle, and breathe. Think of a verdict you reached recently, fast. About a coworker, a relative, a stranger, someone online. Put it on hold, like the old court. Ask: what might I not know? What would a good lawyer for this person say? You don't have to change your mind. Just let the verdict wait until tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Be slow to judge. The first saying of the Great Assembly in Avot: be deliberate in judgment, measured and patient.
Your line: judge slowly. Today, the next time you feel a verdict forming about someone, count to ten, and look for one thing in their favor. Day two hundred thirty-four.

235.title: Three pillars (Avot 1:2)
235.hook: Simon the Just: the world stands on Torah, worship and deeds of kindness
235.howItsDone: Torah study, daily prayer and gemilut chasadim structure much of traditional Jewish life, and Simon the Just's saying is often sung, in Hebrew, as a well-known song in Jewish schools and camps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Great Assembly's first advice: be deliberate in judgment. Your line was judge slowly. Did you let one verdict wait? Today, one of the last members of that Assembly gets his own saying. Day two hundred thirty-five.

Try sitting on a two-legged stool. You can do it, for a while, if you concentrate, with your feet planted. But the minute you relax, you tip. Add a third leg and suddenly you can sit there all afternoon without thinking about it. Three is the smallest number that stands on its own. A lot of lives are two-legged stools. All work and worship, no kindness. All kindness, no learning. Leaning hard, one bad day from tipping over. An old sage named Simon had a theory about what the whole world rests on. Today: the three legs.
screen: `A TWO-LEGGED STOOL.` → `THREE STANDS ON ITS OWN.` → `WHAT THE WORLD RESTS ON.`

segments.voice: Simon the Just, Shimon HaTzaddik, was a high priest, and Avot says he was one of the last of the Great Assembly. His saying is the most quoted in the book: on three things the world stands. On Torah. On avodah, worship. And on gemilut chasadim, deeds of loving-kindness. Torah is learning: studying, asking, understanding. Avodah, in Simon's day, meant the service in the Temple in Jerusalem, the offerings he himself performed as high priest. Gemilut chasadim is kindness you do with your hands and time: visiting the sick, comforting mourners, lending without interest, helping a bride, burying the dead. Then something unthinkable happened. In the year seventy, Rome destroyed the Temple. One of the three pillars fell. How does the world stand now? The rabbis gave two answers. First, avodah became prayer. The Talmud calls prayer the service of the heart. Second, an old story tells of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai walking past the ruins with his student, who cried: the place where our sins were atoned is destroyed. And the teacher said, don't grieve, we have another way, just as good: deeds of loving-kindness. And he quoted the prophet Hosea, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." So the three legs are still there. Learning, prayer, kindness. And the stool only stands when all three touch the ground.
screen: `SIMON THE JUST, HIGH PRIEST.` · `TORAH, AVODAH, KINDNESS.` · `THE TEMPLE FALLS IN THE YEAR 70.` · `I DESIRE MERCY, NOT SACRIFICE.` · then, large: `THREE LEGS TO STAND ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one of each today. Settle, and breathe. First leg, learning: what's one thing you'll read or ask about today? Second leg, worship or attention: when will you pause, for a prayer if you pray, or a quiet minute if you don't? Third leg, kindness: whose day can you make lighter with your hands or your time? Picture all three. The bell holds the time.
Three pillars. Simon the Just's saying in Avot: the world stands on Torah, on worship, and on deeds of loving-kindness.
Your line: three legs to stand on. Before bed tonight, check: did I learn something, pause for something, and do something kind? Day two hundred thirty-five.
